questions.prompt: Why is the token bucket algorithm so widely used for rate limiting?

options.text: It allows short bursts up to the bucket capacity while enforcing a steady average rate

questions.explanation: A token bucket refills at a steady rate up to a capacity, so a client can burst up to the bucket size but is held to a steady long-run rate.

questions.prompt: What is the boundary-burst problem with fixed-window rate limiting?

options.text: A client can send a full window just before the reset and another full window just after, briefly doubling the rate

questions.explanation: Because the counter resets at the window boundary, a client can pack a full window on each side of the boundary, sending roughly double the intended rate in a short span.

questions.prompt: What HTTP status code should a rate-limited request receive?
questions.explanation: 429 Too Many Requests signals rate limiting, ideally with a Retry-After header so well-behaved clients back off.

questions.prompt: Which are typical responsibilities of an API gateway? Select all that apply.

options.text: Authentication and rate limiting at the edge
Storing the primary copy of all business data

questions.explanation: A gateway handles cross-cutting concerns: routing, auth, rate limiting, TLS, and observability. It should not become the system of record for business data.

questions.prompt: You run 5 gateway instances, each enforcing '600/minute per user' with a local counter. What goes wrong?

options.text: A user can hit each instance separately, getting up to 5x the intended limit

questions.explanation: Local counters don't coordinate, so a user spread across N instances gets N times the limit. A shared counter (e.g., in Redis) enforces one global limit.

questions.prompt: How does a leaky bucket differ from a token bucket?

options.text: A leaky bucket allows unlimited bursts
A leaky bucket queues requests and processes them at a fixed rate, smoothing bursts into a steady stream
A leaky bucket never limits anything

questions.explanation: A leaky bucket drains at a constant rate, smoothing bursts (with queuing delay), while a token bucket permits bursts up to its capacity.
